title: Named arguments and especially named optional arguments
body:
This is a special case of #92.

Non-named boolean parameters are kind of a pain. Consider HTML's [obtain a worker/worklet agent](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#obtaining-a-worker/worklet-agent). Call sites for it look like:

> Return the result of obtaining a worker/worklet agent given _outside settings_, _isShared_, and true.

You have to go refer to the algorithm to find out what the true is. (It's "can block".) This is kind of bad, and [is discouraged in programming languages](https://ariya.io/2011/08/hall-of-api-shame-boolean-trap). Perhaps worse, you might think that the second argument is about being shared or not, but really what's happening is that we're passing in the value of _isShared_ for the _isTopLevel_ parameter to the original algorithm. The fact that the second argument is about top-levelness is totally lost.

I can imagine a variety of solutions:

0. Do nothing, and continue without named parameters.

1. Define a struct, e.g. containing "is top level" and "can block", and require callers to construct such a struct. Example: [navigation params](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#navigation-params). This is not great; it's heavyweight for the caller, and feels like an abuse of structs.

2. Pass an Infra map. E.g. "Return the result of obtaining a worker/worklet agent given _outside settings_, «[ "is top level" → _isShared_, "can block" → true ]»." This is unprecedented, and feels like a bit of an abuse of maps, but maybe OK?

3. Define a new pattern for named parameters. For example:

	> To **obtain a worker/worklet agent**, given an environment settings object or null _outside settings_, a boolean **is top level**, and a boolean **can block**:
	> 1. Let _agentCluster_ be null.
	> 2. If [is top level] is true, then set _agentCluster_ to a new [agent cluster].
	> 3. ...
	>
	> and later someone uses it:
	>> ... return the result of [obtaining a worker/worklet agent] given _outside settings_, [is top level] set to _isShared_, and [can block] set to true.

	(here using bold to denote what would be `<dfn>`s, and brackets to denote what would be `<a>`s.)
	
	What I mildly dislike about this is that we no longer have variable names for some of our arguments; instead we refer to some of them with links. That's a bit weird. Maybe there's a fix?

What do people think of these?

----

This problem becomes more urgent when you want to have optional named parameters. HTML's [navigate](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#navigate) already has one ("exceptions enabled flag"), and would benefit from at least two more, in its current formulation: replacement enabled (boolean), and navigation type ("form-submission" or "other"). Optionality seems important here; it would be very nice if we didn't have to pass "other" every time we had a non-form-submission navigation.

Of the above solutions, most of them work pretty well with optional named parameters. (1) could define defaults in its struct definition. (2) and (3) would involve some work in the algorithm to say something about if the map entry doesn't exist/the argument wasn't passed, then pick a default.

There is one other solution for this particular problem, though, which might be worth keeping in mind: define wrapper algorithms. So for example, we could define "internal navigate" which takes a non-optional navigation type, and then define "navigate" which calls "internal navigate" with navigation type of "other", and "form navigate" which calls "internal navigate" with navigation type of "form-submission". This might be a good thing, e.g. "form navigate" might never use replacement enabled or exceptions enabled. But in the general case it might be a bad thing; if all parameters are independent, then this leads to a combinatorial explosion of wrapper algorithms (imagine "form-replacement-with-exceptions navigate" vs. "form-replacement navigate" vs. "form navigate" vs. "form-with-exceptions navigate").

---

Anyway, it'd be good to straighten this out, as we start tidying up navigation in HTML.
